Ibn Mas'ud recited: "That, because Allah is the Ally (waliyy) of those who believe." Qatadah said: it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

Indeed Allah ﴿will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. The explanation of this verse has already been given in more than one place, and the manner in which the rivers flow beneath the gardens has already been mentioned. The sentence is brought to explain Allah's guardianship (wilaya) over the believers. ﴿But those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat﴾, that is, they enjoy the goods of this world and benefit from them, as if they were cattle, having no concern except their bellies and their private parts, heedless of the outcome, careless of what they are in. ﴿And the Fire is their abode﴾, that is, a place where they will dwell, a station where they will alight and settle. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new sentence.

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah﴾, that he said: "They are the people of Makkah, Quraysh; it was revealed concerning them."
﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: he said: "They are the people of Madinah, the Ansar." ﴿And He has set right their state (bal)﴾: he said: "their affair."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿He will make their deeds go astray﴾: he said: "They had deeds that were of merit, but Allah does not accept any deed with disbelief."

Al-Nahhas also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾: he said: "Allah made the Prophet and the believers free to choose regarding the prisoners: if they wished, they could kill them; if they wished, they could enslave them; and if they wished, they could ransom them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him regarding the verse: he said: "This is abrogated (mansukh); it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾ (al-Tawbah: 5)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "Prisoners were brought to al-Hajjaj, and he handed to Ibn Umar a man to kill. Ibn Umar said: 'We were not commanded with this. Allah only said: ﴿Until, when you have thoroughly subdued them, then tie the bonds, and then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾.'"

Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Layth who said: "I said to Mujahid: 'It has reached me that Ibn Abbas said: killing prisoners is not permitted, because Allah said: ﴿Then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾.'" Mujahid said: "Pay no attention to this at all. I met the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and all of them denied this and said: 'This is abrogated; it was only during the truce that existed between the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and the polytheists. But today, no: Allah says: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 5), and He says: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾.' If they are among the polytheists of the Arabs, nothing from them is accepted except Islam; if they do not embrace Islam, then killing. As for others than them, when they are taken as prisoners, the Muslims have the choice: if they wish, they may kill them; if they wish, they may spare them; and if they wish, they may ransom them, provided they do not convert from their religion. If they outwardly profess Islam, they are not to be ransomed."

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade killing a child, a woman, or an old man who is decrepit.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who said: "It is about to happen that whoever among you lives will meet Isa, son of Maryam, as a guide (imam) who is rightly guided (mahdi) and a just judge (hakam), and he will break the cross, kill the swine, the jizya will be abolished, and war will lay down its burdens."

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Salamah ibn Nufayl, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), in a hadith, that he said: "War will not lay down its burdens until Yajuj and Majuj come out."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas (p-1374) regarding ﴿And for the disbelievers there are the like thereof﴾: he said: "For the disbelievers of your people, O Muhammad, is the like of what befell the towns that were destroyed, so they will be destroyed by the sword."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2):

It is also called Surat al-Qital (The Chapter of Fighting) and Surat alladhina kafaru (The Chapter of Those Who Disbelieve).

It has thirty-nine verses, though it is said to have thirty-eight, and it is Medinan. Al-Mawardi said: "It is Medinan according to all, except Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, who said: 'Except for one verse of it, which was revealed after the Farewell Pilgrimage, when [the Prophet] left Mecca and kept looking at the House while weeping in grief over it, so there was revealed His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town, which is mightier in strength than your town which has driven you out, have We destroyed, and there was none to help them﴾ [Muhammad: 13].'" Al-Tha'labi said: "It is Meccan."

Ibn Hibat Allah reported this from al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but it is an erroneous statement, for the surah is Medinan, as is not hidden.

Ibn al-Duraysi has related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Qital was revealed in Medina."

Al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from him, who said: "Surat Muhammad was revealed in Medina."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat alladhina kafaru was revealed in Medina."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Ibn 'Imran that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite to them in the Maghrib prayer: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who disbelieved in Allah and barred themselves and others from the way of Allah, which is the religion of Islam, by forbidding them from entering it. So said Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ is: from the House of Allah, by preventing those who intend it.

It is also said that they are the People of the Book, and the relative pronoun is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾, i.e., He nullified them and made them lost.

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of ﴿He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾ is: He nullified their scheming and their plotting against the Prophet (ﷺ), and placed the calamity upon them for their disbelief.

It is also said: He nullified what they did in disbelief of the things they used to call noble character traits, such as maintaining family ties, freeing captives, and hospitality to guests. These, even though they are void in their origin, the meaning is that He, glorified is He, has judged them to be void.

When He mentioned the group of disbelievers, He followed them with mention of the group of believers, saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾. The apparent meaning of this is generality, so every believer who does righteous deeds is included under it, and the specific cause of its revelation does not prevent this. It has been said that it was revealed concerning the Ansar, and it was said concerning some people of Quraysh, and it was said concerning believers among the People of the Book, but what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. And He, glorified is He, singled out belief in what was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) by mention, although it is included under the general belief mentioned before it, as an alert to its nobility and the loftiness of its station. The clause ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the subject, which is His saying "and those who believe," and its predicate, which is His saying ﴿He will remove from them their misdeeds﴾. The meaning of its being "the truth" is that it abrogates what came before it. His saying "from their Lord" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning of ﴿He will remove from them their misdeeds﴾ is: the misdeeds they committed in the past, for He forgave them by means of faith and righteous deed. ﴿And He will amend their condition﴾, i.e., their affair and their state.

Mujahid said: "their affair." Qatada said: "their state." It was also said: "their matter." The meanings are close.

Al-Mubarrad said: "al-bal here means the state."

It was said: the meaning is that He protected them from sins during their lives and guided them to acts of goodness, and the intended meaning is not the amendment of the state of their worldly life, such as giving them wealth and the like. Al-Naqqash said: the meaning is that He amended their intentions. From this is the saying of the poet:

"If you turn toward me with affection, I shall turn toward you with the like of it; and if you turn away, I shall go off to a state of ruin."

The reference in His saying "that" is to what has passed of what He threatened the disbelievers with and promised the believers, and it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is what follows it.

It is also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject: i.e., the matter is that, because of ﴿that those who disbelieve follow falsehood, and that those who believe follow the truth from their Lord﴾. So falsehood is shirk, and truth is monotheism and faith. The meaning is that this causing of the deeds of the disbelievers to go astray is due to their following falsehood, which is associating partners with Allah and acting in disobedience to Him; and that expiation of the sins of the believers and amending of their state is due to their following the truth which Allah commanded them to follow, namely monotheism, faith, and performing acts of obedience. ﴿Thus Allah sets forth for the people their parables﴾, i.e., in the manner of that striking, He makes clear to the people their parables: i.e., the conditions of the two groups, which are like parables in their strangeness.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Thus He sets forth" — Allah makes clear to the people the parables of the good deeds of the believers and the misguiding of the deeds of the disbelievers; that is, whoever is a disbeliever, Allah causes his deed to go astray, and whoever is a believer, Allah expiates his misdeeds.

﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then [it is] striking of the necks﴾. When He, glorified is He, had explained the condition of the two groups, He commanded jihad against the disbelievers. By "those who disbelieve" is meant the polytheists and whoever among the People of the Book is not under a covenant. The accusative of "striking" (ḍarba) is as an infinitive of an omitted verb.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., strike the necks, striking. He singled out the necks for mention because killing most often occurs by severing them. It was also said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (ighra').

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is like their saying: "O self, be patient." It was also said that the implied meaning is: aim at striking the necks.

It was also said: He specified striking the necks because in expressing it there is a harshness and severity that is not in killing itself, namely cutting the throat and separating the limb which is the head of the body, its highest point and the best of its members. ﴿Until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them﴾, i.e., you have gone to excess in killing them and have made killing among them abundant. This is a limit (ghaya) for the command to strike the necks, not for explaining the limit of killing. It is derived from "a thick thing," i.e., coarse; and the verification of its meaning has passed in Surat al-Anfal. ﴿Then bind the bonds﴾. "Wathaq" with a fatha, and it may be with a kasra, is the name of the thing with which one is bound, like a rope. Al-Jawhari said: "wathaqahu" means "he tied him," and he said: "al-withaq with a kasra on the waw is a dialect of it."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿fashuddu﴾ with a damma on the shin, and al-Sulami read it with a kasra.

Allah, glorified is He, only commanded the binding of the bonds so that they would not escape. The meaning is: when you have gone to excess in killing them, then take them captive and bind them with bonds. ﴿Then either [grant] favor afterward or ransom﴾, i.e., either you grant them favor after capture, or you take ransom. "Favor" (manna) is release without compensation, and "ransom" (fida') is what a captive pays to redeem himself from captivity. Killing is not mentioned here, being sufficed by what preceded.

The majority read ﴿fida'an﴾ with the long vowel.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿fidan﴾ with the short vowel. He placed favor before ransom because it is among the noble traits of character, and for this reason the Arabs used to boast of it, as their poet said:

"We do not kill the captives, but we release them, when the burden of debts weighs heavy on the necks."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the limit for that, saying: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾. The burdens of war, which cannot be sustained except by them, are of weapons and mounts. He attributed the laying down to it, although it belongs to its people, in the manner of metaphor. The meaning is that the Muslims are given the choice among those matters until a limit, which is that there be no war with the disbelievers.

Mujahid said: the meaning is "until there is no religion other than the religion of Islam," and al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said likewise.

Al-Kisa'i said: "until people submit." Al-Farra' said: "until they believe and disbelief goes away."

It was also said: the meaning is that the warring enemies lay down their burdens, which is their weapons, by defeat or by truce.

It is related from al-Hasan and 'Ata' that they said: in the verse there is inversion; the meaning is: "striking of the necks until the war lays down its burdens, then when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, bind the bonds."

The scholars have differed concerning this verse: is it muhkam (definitive) or mansukh (abrogated)? It was said that it is abrogated concerning the idolaters, and that it is not permissible to ransom them or to show them favor. The abrogating text is His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and His saying: ﴿So if you overpower them in war, then disperse those behind them﴾ [al-Anfal: 57], and His saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. This is the view of Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, and many of the Kufans, who said: "al-Ma'ida is the last thing revealed, so every polytheist must be killed except those for whom there is evidence of leaving them, such as women and children, and those from whom the jizya is taken." This is the well-known position of Abu Hanifa.

It was also said that this verse abrogates His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. This was related from 'Ata' and others.

Many scholars said: the verse is muhkam, and the imam is free to choose between killing and taking captives, and after capture is free to choose between favor and ransom. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu 'Ubayd, and others.

This is the preponderant view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the rightly-guided Caliphs after him did this.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: there is no ransom or capture except after inflicting slaughter and killing by the sword, because of His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]. So if he captures after that, the imam may decide what he sees fit, whether killing or otherwise.

﴿That [is the command]. And had Allah willed, He could have avenged Himself upon them﴾. The position of "that" is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: i.e., the matter is that. It was also said that it is in the accusative position as an object by an implied verb: i.e., do that. It may also be a subject whose predicate is omitted, indicated by what preceded: i.e., that is the ruling concerning the disbelievers. The meaning of ﴿And had Allah willed, He could have avenged Himself upon them﴾ is: He is capable of taking revenge upon them, by punishing them and destroying them and torturing them with whatever kinds of punishment He wills; but He commanded you to fight them ﴿so that He may test some of you by means of others﴾, i.e., to test some of you by others, that He may know those who strive in His way and those who are patient under His trial, reward them abundantly, and punish the disbelievers at their hands.

﴿And those who were killed in the way of Allah﴾. The majority read "qatalu" (they fought) with the active voice. Abu 'Amr and Hafs read "qutilu" (were killed) in the passive voice. al-Hasan read it with the doubling of the consonant, also in the passive voice.

Al-Jahdari, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Abu Haywa read "qatalu" in the active voice without the alif and with lightening. The meaning according to the first and fourth readings is that the strivers in the way of Allah, their reward is not lost; and according to the second and third readings, that those killed in the way of Allah likewise—Allah, glorified is He, does not waste their reward.

Qatada said: it was mentioned to us that this verse was revealed on the day of Uhud.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what they have with Him of abundant reward, saying: ﴿He will guide them﴾, i.e., Allah, glorified is He, will guide them to right conduct in this world and will give them reward in the Hereafter. ﴿And amend their condition﴾, i.e., their state, their affair, and their matter.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: guidance may occur, and what is meant by it is guiding the believers to the paths of the Gardens and the way leading to them. Ibn Ziyad said: He guides them to the argument with Munkar and Nakir.

﴿And admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾, i.e., He made it clear to them until they recognized it without inference. That is because when they enter Paradise, they disperse to their dwellings.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of the majority of the commentators.

Al-Hasan said: Allah described Paradise to them in this world, so when they entered it, they recognized it by its description.

It was also said that there is an ellipsis: i.e., they recognized its paths, its dwellings, and its houses.

It was also said: this "making known" is by a sign that guides them to it, namely the angel assigned to the servant who walks before him until he brings him to his abode. So said Muqatil.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿which He has made known to them﴾ is that He made it fragrant with various delights, taken from "al-'arf," which is fragrance.

Then He promised them, may He be exalted, victory for His religion in His words: ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you﴾. That is: if you help the religion of Allah, He will help you against the disbelievers and grant you victory. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾.

Qutrub said: "If you help the Prophet of Allah, He will help you." ﴿And make your feet firm﴾, that is, at the time of fighting. Making the feet firm is an expression for victory and assistance in the places of war. It was also said: "upon Islam," and it was said: "upon the path (al-Sirat)."

﴿But as for those who disbelieve, for them is ruin (ta'san)﴾. The relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, its implied form being "fa-ta'isu" ("so let them stumble"), as indicated by what follows it. The fa' (fa) was introduced to make the subject resemble a conditional clause. The accusative of ta'san is as an infinitive (masdar) for the implied verb which serves as the predicate.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like 'suqya' for them and 'ra'ya' for them." The root of ta's is downfall and stumbling.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "Ta's is to be dragged upon one's face, and naks is to be dragged upon one's head." He said: "Ta's also means destruction."

Al-Jawhari said: "Its origin is to be overturned, which is the opposite of being raised up." From this is the verse of Mujammi' ibn Hilal:
She says, when I had separated her from her husband: "You have stumbled, as you made me stumble, O Mujammi'."

Al-Mubarrad said: that is, "so for them is something hateful." Ibn Jurayj said: "distance (bu'dan) for them." Al-Suddi said: "disgrace for them."

Ibn Zayd said: "misery for them."

Al-Hasan said: "cursing for them."

Tha'lab said: "destruction for them." Al-Dahhak said: "failure for them." Abu al-Aliyah said: "wretchedness for them," as related by al-Naqqash.

Al-Dahhak said: "humiliation for them."

Tha'lab also said: "evil for them."

Abu al-Aliyah said: "wretchedness for them."

The lam in "lahum" is for clarification, as in His saying: ﴿Hayta laka﴾ (Yusuf: 23). His saying ﴿and He will make their deeds go astray﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it and is included with it in the informative nature of the relative clause.

The demonstrative in His saying "that" (dhalika) refers to what was previously mentioned of ruin and misguidance: that is, "the matter is that," or "that matter" ﴿because they disliked what Allah has sent down﴾, namely the Qur'an sent down to His Messenger, or what He sent down to His messengers of scriptures, since they contain what is in the Qur'an of monotheism and resurrection. So Allah made their deeds fruitless because of that cause. What is meant by "deeds" is what they had done of good works in outward form, even though they were false from the outset, since the deed of a disbeliever is not accepted before he becomes Muslim.

Then He, may He be exalted, warned the disbelievers and guided them to take a lesson from the condition of those before them, so He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land﴾, that is: have they not travelled through the land of 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lut, and others, so that they might take warning, ﴿and see how was the end of those before them﴾, that is, the final outcome of the disbelievers before them, for the traces of punishment remain in their dwellings.

Then He, may He be exalted, explained what He did to those before them, so He said: ﴿Allah destroyed them utterly﴾. The sentence is a new (resumptive) clause answering an implied question. Tadmir and halak mean destruction: that is, He destroyed them and uprooted them. It is said: "dammarahu" and "dammara 'alayhi" with the same meaning.

Then He threatened the idolaters of Makkah, so He said: ﴿And for the disbelievers there are the like thereof﴾, that is, for these disbelievers there are like the outcome of those disbelieving nations before them.

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jarir said: the pronoun in "amthaliha" (its like) refers to the end of those before them. It is in the plural because the outcomes are many according to the number of punished nations. It was also said: the like of the punishment; it was also said: destruction; it was also said: the act of destroying. The first (view) is preferable because the pronoun refers to what is mentioned before it.

The demonstrative in His saying "that" refers to what was mentioned, that for the disbelievers there are like thereof, ﴿because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe﴾, that is, because Allah is the helper of them, ﴿and that the disbelievers have no protector (mawla)﴾, that is, no helper who can repel (punishment) from them.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "That, because Allah is the Ally (waliyy) of those who believe." Qatadah said: it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

Indeed Allah ﴿will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. The explanation of this verse has already been given in more than one place, and the manner in which the rivers flow beneath the gardens has already been mentioned. The sentence is brought to explain Allah's guardianship (wilaya) over the believers. ﴿But those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat﴾, that is, they enjoy the goods of this world and benefit from them, as if they were cattle, having no concern except their bellies and their private parts, heedless of the outcome, careless of what they are in. ﴿And the Fire is their abode﴾, that is, a place where they will dwell, a station where they will alight and settle. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new sentence.

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah﴾, that he said: "They are the people of Makkah, Quraysh; it was revealed concerning them."
﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: he said: "They are the people of Madinah, the Ansar." ﴿And He has set right their state (bal)﴾: he said: "their affair."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿He will make their deeds go astray﴾: he said: "They had deeds that were of merit, but Allah does not accept any deed with disbelief."

Al-Nahhas also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾: he said: "Allah made the Prophet and the believers free to choose regarding the prisoners: if they wished, they could kill them; if they wished, they could enslave them; and if they wished, they could ransom them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him regarding the verse: he said: "This is abrogated (mansukh); it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾ (al-Tawbah: 5)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "Prisoners were brought to al-Hajjaj, and he handed to Ibn Umar a man to kill. Ibn Umar said: 'We were not commanded with this. Allah only said: ﴿Until, when you have thoroughly subdued them, then tie the bonds, and then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾.'"

Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Layth who said: "I said to Mujahid: 'It has reached me that Ibn Abbas said: killing prisoners is not permitted, because Allah said: ﴿Then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾.'" Mujahid said: "Pay no attention to this at all. I met the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and all of them denied this and said: 'This is abrogated; it was only during the truce that existed between the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and the polytheists. But today, no: Allah says: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 5), and He says: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾.' If they are among the polytheists of the Arabs, nothing from them is accepted except Islam; if they do not embrace Islam, then killing. As for others than them, when they are taken as prisoners, the Muslims have the choice: if they wish, they may kill them; if they wish, they may spare them; and if they wish, they may ransom them, provided they do not convert from their religion. If they outwardly profess Islam, they are not to be ransomed."

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade killing a child, a woman, or an old man who is decrepit.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who said: "It is about to happen that whoever among you lives will meet Isa, son of Maryam, as a guide (imam) who is rightly guided (mahdi) and a just judge (hakam), and he will break the cross, kill the swine, the jizya will be abolished, and war will lay down its burdens."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas (p-1374) regarding ﴿And for the disbelievers there are the like thereof﴾: he said: "For the disbelievers of your people, O Muhammad, is the like of what befell the towns that were destroyed, so they will be destroyed by the sword."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 19–28 (part 1 of 2):

He, glory be to Him, warned the disbelievers that He had destroyed those who were stronger than them, so He said: ﴿And how many a town, stronger in power than your town which has expelled you, have We destroyed; and they had no helper﴾. We have already shown that *ka'ayyin* (كَأيِّنْ) is composed of the *kaf* and *ayy* (أيٌّ), and that it has the meaning of the interrogative-informative *kam* ("how many"), i.e. "and how many a town." Al-Akhfash cited the verse of al-Walid:

*How many kings and commoners have we seen,*
*and a key to the shackles of the bound prisoner.*

The meaning of the verse is: "And how many a people of a town were stronger than the people of your town which expelled you, We destroyed them. ﴿So there was no helper for them﴾." Then, *a fortiori*, [the same applies to] those who are weaker than them, namely the Quraysh, who are the people of the town of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is Makkah. The speech is therefore elliptical (omitting a *mudaf*), as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. Muqatil said: that is, "We destroyed them with punishment when they denied their messenger."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the difference between the condition of the believer and the condition of the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾. The *hamza* is for rebuke, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied clause, as in its counterparts. *Man* (مَن) is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾. [The predicate] is singular in this case in view of the wording of *man*, and plural in His saying ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in view of its meaning. The meaning is that one who is upon certainty from his Lord is not equal to, and is not like, one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, which is the worship of idols, associating partners with Allah, and acting in disobedience to Allah. "And they followed their desires" in worshipping them, and they immersed themselves in kinds of misguidance without any doubt that would warrant suspicion, let alone a clear proof.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had explained the difference between the two groups in guidance and misguidance, He explained the difference in their destination and their end, so He said: ﴿The description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. The sentence is a new (resumptive) clause, to explain the excellences of the Garden and what is in it. The meaning of ﴿description (*mathal*)﴾ is its wondrous quality. It is the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: its supposed predicate is "what they hear." Sibawayh supposed it to be "what is recited to you is the description of the Garden." He said: *mathal* means description, and its meaning is "the description of the Garden." The clause ﴿therein are rivers of water unchanging﴾ etc. explains the *mathal*.

It was also said that *mathal* is superfluous. It was also said that ﴿the description of the Garden﴾ is the subject, and the predicate is "therein are rivers." It was also said that its predicate is ﴿like one who abides forever﴾.

*Al-asin* means "that which has changed." It is said: "the water became *asin* (آسِنَ) yā'sanu (يَأْسَنُ) *usūnan* (أُسُونًا)," when its smell has changed. Similar is *al-ājin* (الآجِنُ). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I shall leave the horn with its fingertips yellowed,*
*swaying on the spear like the swaying of brackish, changed water.*

The majority of readers recited *āsin* (آسِنٍ) with the long vowel (*madd*). Humayd and Ibn Kathir recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*); both are dialects, like *ḥādhir* and *ḥadhir*.

Al-Akhfash said: the long form is intended for the future, and the short form is intended for the present.

﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾: that is, it does not turn sour as the milk of this world does, because it did not come out from the udders of camels, sheep and cattle.

﴿And rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾: that is, delicious to them, pleasant to drink, which the drinkers do not find distasteful. It is said: *sharāb ladhdh* (شَرابٌ لَذٌّ) and *ladhīdh* (لَذِيذٌ), and *fīhi ladhdha* (فِيهِ لَذَّةٌ) with the same meaning. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers﴾ [al-Saffat: 46]. The majority recited *ladhdhatin* (لَذَّةٍ) with the genitive, as an adjective of *khamr*. It was also read with the accusative as a *masdar* or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). It was also read with the nominative as an adjective of *anhār*.

﴿And rivers of honey, purified﴾: that is, purified from what mixes with it of wax, debris, dregs and sediment. ﴿And for them therein is every kind of fruit﴾: that is, for the people of the Garden in the Garden, along with what has been mentioned of the drinks, is every kind of fruit; that is, every category of its categories. *Min* (مِن) is superfluous for emphasis. ﴿And forgiveness from their Lord﴾ for their sins. The indefiniteness of *maghfira* (مَغْفِرَةٌ) is for magnification: that is, for them is a great forgiveness, coming from their Lord.

﴿Like one who abides forever in the Fire﴾: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the supposed meaning is: "Is it then one who is in the bliss of the Garden in this description, abiding forever therein, like one who abides forever in the Fire?" Or it is the predicate of His saying "the description of the Garden," as preceded.

Al-Farra' preferred the first, saying: he intended "Is he who is in this bliss like one who abides forever in the Fire?"

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, "Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord, and is given these things, like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, and who abides forever in the Fire?" So His saying "like one" (كَمَن) is a substitution for His saying ﴿Is he for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾.

Ibn Kaysan said: the description of the Garden in which are fruits and rivers is not like the description of the Fire in which are boiling water and *zaqqum*; and the description of the people of the Garden in bliss is not like the description of the people of the Fire in painful torment.

His saying: ﴿and they are given boiling water to drink﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause (*silah*). He coordinated a verbal clause with a nominal clause, but he observed in the first the wording of *man* and in the second its meaning. *Hamim* is hot water of intense boiling. When they drink it, it cuts their intestines, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so that it cuts their bowels﴾, because of its extreme heat.

*Al-am'a'* is the plural of *ma'an* (مِعًى), and it is what is in the bellies of the intestines.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾: that is, among these disbelievers who enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, ﴿those who listen to you﴾, and they are the hypocrites. He made the pronoun singular in view of the wording of *man*, and plural in His saying ﴿until, when they go out from you﴾ in view of its meaning. The meaning is that the hypocrites used to attend the places of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) admonition and the occasions of his sermons, which he dictated to the Muslims, until, when they went out from him, ﴿they said to those who were given knowledge﴾. They were the scholars among the Companions. It was said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas; it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud; it was said: Abu al-Darda'. The first is preferred. That is, they asked the people of knowledge, and said to them: ﴿What did he say just now?﴾ That is, what did the Prophet say just now, in the manner of mockery. The meaning is: "We did not pay attention to his words." *Ānifan* (آنِفًا) is intended to mean "just now," the nearest of times. From it comes *amrun ānif* (أمْرٌ آنِفٌ), that is, a newly begun matter (مُسْتَأْنَفٌ) [p. 1375]; and *rawḍatun unuf* (رَوْضَةٌ أُنُفٌ), that is, a meadow no one has grazed. Its accusative is as an adverb of time: that is, a newly begun time; or it is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in *qāla* (قالَ).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *istannaftu al-shay'* (اسْتَأْنَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ), when you begin something. Its origin is taken from the nose (*anf*) of a thing, for what has preceded from it, borrowed from the organ. From it is the saying of the poet:

*And the secret of their neighbour is forbidden to them,*
*and their neighbour eats the nose of the dishes.*

The indication of His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to those mentioned of the hypocrites: ﴿those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾, so they do not believe, and their hearts do not turn toward any good; ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in disbelief and obstinacy.

Then He mentioned the condition of their opposites, so He said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. That is, those who were guided to the path of good, so they believed in Allah and acted upon what He commanded them, He increased them in guidance by granting success. It was said: He increased them by the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: He increased them by the Qur'an.

Al-Farra' said: the turning away and mockery of the hypocrites increased them in guidance. It was said: the descent of the abrogating (*nāsikh*) [verse] increased them in guidance. In any case, the meaning is that He increased them in faith, knowledge and insight into the religion. ﴿And gave them their piety﴾: that is, He inspired them with it and helped them to it.

As for *taqwa* (piety), al-Rabi' said: it is fear (*khashya*). Al-Suddi said: it is the reward of the Hereafter. Muqatil said: it is the success to act in what He is pleased with. It was said: acting upon the abrogating [verse] and leaving the abrogated (*mansukh*) one. It was said: leaving the concessions (*rukhas*) and adhering to the firm obligations (*'azā'im*).

﴿Do they then await anything but the Hour﴾: that is, the Resurrection, ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾: that is, unexpectedly. In this there is a severe threat to the disbelievers. His saying ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾ is a substitution for "the Hour," a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*).

Abu Ja'far al-Rawwasi recited *in ta'tihim* (إنْ تَأْتِهِمْ) with the conditional *in* (إنْ). ﴿So its signs have already come﴾: that is, its indications and its marks. They had read in their books that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the last of the prophets, so his being sent is among its signs. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

*Al-ashrat* (الأشْراطُ) is the plural of *shart* (شَرْطٌ), with the *ra'* vowelled both with sukun and with fatha.

It was said: what is meant by "its signs" here is its causes, which are less than its greatest parts.

It was said: he intended by the signs of the Hour the splitting of the moon and the smoke; so said al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: the abundance of wealth and trade, false testimony, the severing of kinship ties, the scarcity of the noble and the abundance of the base. From it is the saying of Abu Zayd al-Aswad:

*If you have indeed resolved on severing between us,*
*then the signs of its beginning have already appeared.*

﴿Then how will there be for them, when their reminder comes to them?﴾ "Their reminder" (ذِكْراهم) is the subject, and its predicate is "then how will there be for them," that is: how will there be for them the remembrance when the Hour comes to them, as in His saying: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance be for him?﴾ [al-Fajr: 23]. And "when it comes to them" is a parenthetical clause between the subject and the predicate.

﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾: that is, if you know that the basis of good is monotheism and obedience, and the basis of evil is associating partners with Allah and acting in disobedience to Allah, then know that there is no god besides Him and no lord other than Him. The meaning is: "Remain firm upon that and persist in it," because he (ﷺ) had already known before this that there is no god but Allah. It was said: "what you know by inference, know it as certain knowledge." It was also said the meaning is: "Remember that there is no god but Allah," so he expressed remembrance by knowledge.

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾: that is, ask Allah forgiveness that any sin should occur from you, or ask Allah that He preserve you, or ask Him forgiveness for what may perhaps proceed from you of leaving the better course (*tark al-awla*).

It was said the address is to him, and the intended meaning is his community. This is rejected by His saying ﴿and for the believing men and believing women﴾, for its meaning is his asking forgiveness for the sins of his community by supplicating for them to be forgiven for what has passed of their sins.

﴿And Allah knows your movement﴾ in your deeds, ﴿and your resting place﴾ in the abode of the Hereafter. It was also said: your movement in your deeds by day, and your resting place in your night while you sleep.

It was said: your movement in the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers, and your resting place on the earth, that is, your dwelling in it.

Ibn Kaysan said: your movement from back to belly in this world, and your resting place in the graves.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) left Makkah for the cave, he turned toward Makkah and said: "You are the dearest of Allah's lands to me. Had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left. The most wicked of enemies is one who transgresses against Allah in His sanctuary, or kills someone other than his killer, or kills by the custom of the Jahiliyyah." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And how many a town﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿rivers of water unchanging﴾ that he said: "not altered."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* narrated from Mu'awiya ibn Haydah: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "In Paradise there is a sea of milk, a sea of water, a sea of honey and a sea of wine; then the rivers split from them."

Al-Harith ibn Abi Usama in his *Musnad* and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ka'b who said: "The Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, the Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise, the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise, and the Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated through the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿until, when they go out from you, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he say just now?"﴾ that he said: "I was among those who asked."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated by another route from him concerning the verse that he said: "I am among them."

In this there is a great virtue for Ibn 'Abbas, because at that time he was a boy who had not reached puberty, for the Prophet (ﷺ) died when he was of the age of puberty. So people's asking him about the meanings of the Qur'an during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah's description of those who were asked as "those who were given knowledge," of which he was one, is among the greatest proofs of the breadth of his knowledge and the abundance of his understanding of the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, despite his peers and those of his age at that time playing with the children.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that he said: "They used to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when they left his presence they would ask Ibn Abbas: 'What did he say just now?' He would tell them so-and-so. Ibn Abbas was the youngest of the people, so Allah revealed the verse, and Ibn Abbas was among those who were given knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Buraydah concerning the verse that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Mas'ud."

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Mas'ud."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and grants them their piety﴾. He said: "When the Qur'an was revealed, they believed in it, and it was guidance for them. Then, when the abrogating (nasikh, the verse that cancels an earlier ruling) was distinguished from the abrogated (mansukh, the verse whose ruling is cancelled), it increased them in guidance."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning ﴿So its portents have already come﴾ that he said: "The first of the Hours (signs of the Hour)."

It is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he pointed with the middle finger and the index finger. A similar report is in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.

There are many hadiths on this subject explaining the portents of the Hour and what has already occurred of them and what has not yet occurred. They will come in a separate dedicated work, so we will not lengthen the discussion by mentioning them here.

al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The best remembrance is 'There is no god but Allah,' and the best supplication is seeking forgiveness," and then he recited: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times a day."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Sarjis, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ate some food with him. I said: 'May Allah forgive you, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'And you.' It was then said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you ask forgiveness for him?' He said: 'Yes, and for you as well,' and then he recited: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾." Hadiths have also been transmitted about his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for himself and for his community, and about his encouraging seeking forgiveness.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And Allah knows your movement (mutaqallabakum)﴾ that it refers to your movement in this world, and your dwelling (mathwakum) in the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *istannaftu al-shay'* (اسْتَأْنَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ), when you begin something. Its origin is taken from the nose (*anf*) of a thing, for what has preceded from it, borrowed from the organ. From it is the saying of the poet:

*And the secret of their neighbour is forbidden to them,*
*and their neighbour eats the nose of the dishes.*

The indication of His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to those mentioned of the hypocrites: ﴿those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾, so they do not believe, and their hearts do not turn toward any good; ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in disbelief and obstinacy.

Then He mentioned the condition of their opposites, so He said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. That is, those who were guided to the path of good, so they believed in Allah and acted upon what He commanded them, He increased them in guidance by granting success. It was said: He increased them by the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: He increased them by the Qur'an.

Al-Farra' said: the turning away and mockery of the hypocrites increased them in guidance. It was said: the descent of the abrogating (*nāsikh*) [verse] increased them in guidance. In any case, the meaning is that He increased them in faith, knowledge and insight into the religion. ﴿And gave them their piety﴾: that is, He inspired them with it and helped them to it.

As for *taqwa* (piety), al-Rabi' said: it is fear (*khashya*). Al-Suddi said: it is the reward of the Hereafter. Muqatil said: it is the success to act in what He is pleased with. It was said: acting upon the abrogating [verse] and leaving the abrogated (*mansukh*) one. It was said: leaving the concessions (*rukhas*) and adhering to the firm obligations (*'azā'im*).

﴿Do they then await anything but the Hour﴾: that is, the Resurrection, ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾: that is, unexpectedly. In this there is a severe threat to the disbelievers. His saying ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾ is a substitution for "the Hour," a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*).

Abu Ja'far al-Rawwasi recited *in ta'tihim* (إنْ تَأْتِهِمْ) with the conditional *in* (إنْ). ﴿So its signs have already come﴾: that is, its indications and its marks. They had read in their books that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the last of the prophets, so his being sent is among its signs. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

*Al-ashrat* (الأشْراطُ) is the plural of *shart* (شَرْطٌ), with the *ra'* vowelled both with sukun and with fatha.

It was said: what is meant by "its signs" here is its causes, which are less than its greatest parts.

It was said: he intended by the signs of the Hour the splitting of the moon and the smoke; so said al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: the abundance of wealth and trade, false testimony, the severing of kinship ties, the scarcity of the noble and the abundance of the base. From it is the saying of Abu Zayd al-Aswad:

*If you have indeed resolved on severing between us,*
*then the signs of its beginning have already appeared.*

﴿Then how will there be for them, when their reminder comes to them?﴾ "Their reminder" (ذِكْراهم) is the subject, and its predicate is "then how will there be for them," that is: how will there be for them the remembrance when the Hour comes to them, as in His saying: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance be for him?﴾ [al-Fajr: 23]. And "when it comes to them" is a parenthetical clause between the subject and the predicate.

﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾: that is, if you know that the basis of good is monotheism and obedience, and the basis of evil is associating partners with Allah and acting in disobedience to Allah, then know that there is no god besides Him and no lord other than Him. The meaning is: "Remain firm upon that and persist in it," because he (ﷺ) had already known before this that there is no god but Allah. It was said: "what you know by inference, know it as certain knowledge." It was also said the meaning is: "Remember that there is no god but Allah," so he expressed remembrance by knowledge.

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾: that is, ask Allah forgiveness that any sin should occur from you, or ask Allah that He preserve you, or ask Him forgiveness for what may perhaps proceed from you of leaving the better course (*tark al-awla*).

It was said the address is to him, and the intended meaning is his community. This is rejected by His saying ﴿and for the believing men and believing women﴾, for its meaning is his asking forgiveness for the sins of his community by supplicating for them to be forgiven for what has passed of their sins.

﴿And Allah knows your movement﴾ in your deeds, ﴿and your resting place﴾ in the abode of the Hereafter. It was also said: your movement in your deeds by day, and your resting place in your night while you sleep.

It was said: your movement in the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers, and your resting place on the earth, that is, your dwelling in it.

Ibn Kaysan said: your movement from back to belly in this world, and your resting place in the graves.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) left Makkah for the cave, he turned toward Makkah and said: "You are the dearest of Allah's lands to me. Had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left. The most wicked of enemies is one who transgresses against Allah in His sanctuary, or kills someone other than his killer, or kills by the custom of the Jahiliyyah." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And how many a town﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿rivers of water unchanging﴾ that he said: "not altered."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* narrated from Mu'awiya ibn Haydah: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "In Paradise there is a sea of milk, a sea of water, a sea of honey and a sea of wine; then the rivers split from them."

Al-Harith ibn Abi Usama in his *Musnad* and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ka'b who said: "The Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, the Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise, the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise, and the Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated through the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿until, when they go out from you, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he say just now?"﴾ that he said: "I was among those who asked."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated by another route from him concerning the verse that he said: "I am among them."

In this there is a great virtue for Ibn 'Abbas, because at that time he was a boy who had not reached puberty, for the Prophet (ﷺ) died when he was of the age of puberty. So people's asking him about the meanings of the Qur'an during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah's description of those who were asked as "those who were given knowledge," of which he was one, is among the greatest proofs of the breadth of his knowledge and the abundance of his understanding of the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, despite his peers and those of his age at that time playing with the children.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that he said: "They used to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when they left his presence they would ask Ibn Abbas: 'What did he say just now?' He would tell them so-and-so. Ibn Abbas was the youngest of the people, so Allah revealed the verse, and Ibn Abbas was among those who were given knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Buraydah concerning the verse that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Mas'ud."

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Mas'ud."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and grants them their piety﴾. He said: "When the Qur'an was revealed, they believed in it, and it was guidance for them. Then, when the abrogating (nasikh, the verse that cancels an earlier ruling) was distinguished from the abrogated (mansukh, the verse whose ruling is cancelled), it increased them in guidance."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning ﴿So its portents have already come﴾ that he said: "The first of the Hours (signs of the Hour)."

It is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he pointed with the middle finger and the index finger. A similar report is in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.

There are many hadiths on this subject explaining the portents of the Hour and what has already occurred of them and what has not yet occurred. They will come in a separate dedicated work, so we will not lengthen the discussion by mentioning them here.

al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The best remembrance is 'There is no god but Allah,' and the best supplication is seeking forgiveness," and then he recited: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times a day."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Sarjis, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ate some food with him. I said: 'May Allah forgive you, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'And you.' It was then said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you ask forgiveness for him?' He said: 'Yes, and for you as well,' and then he recited: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾." Hadiths have also been transmitted about his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for himself and for his community, and about his encouraging seeking forgiveness.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And Allah knows your movement (mutaqallabakum)﴾ that it refers to your movement in this world, and your dwelling (mathwakum) in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 19–28 (part 1 of 2):

He, glory be to Him, warned the disbelievers that He had destroyed those who were stronger than them, so He said: ﴿And how many a town, stronger in power than your town which has expelled you, have We destroyed; and they had no helper﴾. We have already shown that *ka'ayyin* (كَأيِّنْ) is composed of the *kaf* and *ayy* (أيٌّ), and that it has the meaning of the interrogative-informative *kam* ("how many"), i.e. "and how many a town." Al-Akhfash cited the verse of al-Walid:

*How many kings and commoners have we seen,*
*and a key to the shackles of the bound prisoner.*

The meaning of the verse is: "And how many a people of a town were stronger than the people of your town which expelled you, We destroyed them. ﴿So there was no helper for them﴾." Then, *a fortiori*, [the same applies to] those who are weaker than them, namely the Quraysh, who are the people of the town of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is Makkah. The speech is therefore elliptical (omitting a *mudaf*), as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. Muqatil said: that is, "We destroyed them with punishment when they denied their messenger."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the difference between the condition of the believer and the condition of the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾. The *hamza* is for rebuke, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied clause, as in its counterparts. *Man* (مَن) is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾. [The predicate] is singular in this case in view of the wording of *man*, and plural in His saying ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in view of its meaning. The meaning is that one who is upon certainty from his Lord is not equal to, and is not like, one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, which is the worship of idols, associating partners with Allah, and acting in disobedience to Allah. "And they followed their desires" in worshipping them, and they immersed themselves in kinds of misguidance without any doubt that would warrant suspicion, let alone a clear proof.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had explained the difference between the two groups in guidance and misguidance, He explained the difference in their destination and their end, so He said: ﴿The description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. The sentence is a new (resumptive) clause, to explain the excellences of the Garden and what is in it. The meaning of ﴿description (*mathal*)﴾ is its wondrous quality. It is the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: its supposed predicate is "what they hear." Sibawayh supposed it to be "what is recited to you is the description of the Garden." He said: *mathal* means description, and its meaning is "the description of the Garden." The clause ﴿therein are rivers of water unchanging﴾ etc. explains the *mathal*.

It was also said that *mathal* is superfluous. It was also said that ﴿the description of the Garden﴾ is the subject, and the predicate is "therein are rivers." It was also said that its predicate is ﴿like one who abides forever﴾.

*Al-asin* means "that which has changed." It is said: "the water became *asin* (آسِنَ) yā'sanu (يَأْسَنُ) *usūnan* (أُسُونًا)," when its smell has changed. Similar is *al-ājin* (الآجِنُ). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I shall leave the horn with its fingertips yellowed,*
*swaying on the spear like the swaying of brackish, changed water.*

The majority of readers recited *āsin* (آسِنٍ) with the long vowel (*madd*). Humayd and Ibn Kathir recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*); both are dialects, like *ḥādhir* and *ḥadhir*.

Al-Akhfash said: the long form is intended for the future, and the short form is intended for the present.

﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾: that is, it does not turn sour as the milk of this world does, because it did not come out from the udders of camels, sheep and cattle.

﴿And rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾: that is, delicious to them, pleasant to drink, which the drinkers do not find distasteful. It is said: *sharāb ladhdh* (شَرابٌ لَذٌّ) and *ladhīdh* (لَذِيذٌ), and *fīhi ladhdha* (فِيهِ لَذَّةٌ) with the same meaning. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers﴾ [al-Saffat: 46]. The majority recited *ladhdhatin* (لَذَّةٍ) with the genitive, as an adjective of *khamr*. It was also read with the accusative as a *masdar* or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). It was also read with the nominative as an adjective of *anhār*.

﴿And rivers of honey, purified﴾: that is, purified from what mixes with it of wax, debris, dregs and sediment. ﴿And for them therein is every kind of fruit﴾: that is, for the people of the Garden in the Garden, along with what has been mentioned of the drinks, is every kind of fruit; that is, every category of its categories. *Min* (مِن) is superfluous for emphasis. ﴿And forgiveness from their Lord﴾ for their sins. The indefiniteness of *maghfira* (مَغْفِرَةٌ) is for magnification: that is, for them is a great forgiveness, coming from their Lord.

﴿Like one who abides forever in the Fire﴾: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the supposed meaning is: "Is it then one who is in the bliss of the Garden in this description, abiding forever therein, like one who abides forever in the Fire?" Or it is the predicate of His saying "the description of the Garden," as preceded.

Al-Farra' preferred the first, saying: he intended "Is he who is in this bliss like one who abides forever in the Fire?"

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, "Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord, and is given these things, like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, and who abides forever in the Fire?" So His saying "like one" (كَمَن) is a substitution for His saying ﴿Is he for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾.

Ibn Kaysan said: the description of the Garden in which are fruits and rivers is not like the description of the Fire in which are boiling water and *zaqqum*; and the description of the people of the Garden in bliss is not like the description of the people of the Fire in painful torment.

His saying: ﴿and they are given boiling water to drink﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause (*silah*). He coordinated a verbal clause with a nominal clause, but he observed in the first the wording of *man* and in the second its meaning. *Hamim* is hot water of intense boiling. When they drink it, it cuts their intestines, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so that it cuts their bowels﴾, because of its extreme heat.

*Al-am'a'* is the plural of *ma'an* (مِعًى), and it is what is in the bellies of the intestines.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾: that is, among these disbelievers who enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, ﴿those who listen to you﴾, and they are the hypocrites. The meaning is that the hypocrites used to attend the places of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) admonition and the occasions of his sermons, which he dictated to the Muslims, until, when they went out from him, ﴿they said to those who were given knowledge﴾. They were the scholars among the Companions. It was said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas; it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud; it was said: Abu al-Darda'. The first is preferred. That is, they asked the people of knowledge, and said to them: ﴿What did he say just now?﴾ That is, what did the Prophet say just now, in the manner of mockery. The meaning is: "We did not pay attention to his words." *Ānifan* (آنِفًا) is intended to mean "just now," the nearest of times. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning ﴿So its portents have already come﴾ that he said: "The first of the Hours (signs of the Hour)."

It is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he pointed with the middle finger and the index finger. al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The best remembrance is 'There is no god but Allah,' and the best supplication is seeking forgiveness," and then he recited: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times a day."
