Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 19–28 (part 1 of 2):

He, glory be to Him, warned the disbelievers that He had destroyed those who were stronger than them, so He said: ﴿And how many a town, stronger in power than your town which has expelled you, have We destroyed; and they had no helper﴾. We have already shown that *ka'ayyin* (كَأيِّنْ) is composed of the *kaf* and *ayy* (أيٌّ), and that it has the meaning of the interrogative-informative *kam* ("how many"), i.e. "and how many a town." Al-Akhfash cited the verse of al-Walid:

*How many kings and commoners have we seen,*
*and a key to the shackles of the bound prisoner.*

The meaning of the verse is: "And how many a people of a town were stronger than the people of your town which expelled you, We destroyed them. ﴿So there was no helper for them﴾." Then, *a fortiori*, [the same applies to] those who are weaker than them, namely the Quraysh, who are the people of the town of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is Makkah. The speech is therefore elliptical (omitting a *mudaf*), as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. Muqatil said: that is, "We destroyed them with punishment when they denied their messenger."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the difference between the condition of the believer and the condition of the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾. The *hamza* is for rebuke, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied clause, as in its counterparts. *Man* (مَن) is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾. [The predicate] is singular in this case in view of the wording of *man*, and plural in His saying ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in view of its meaning. The meaning is that one who is upon certainty from his Lord is not equal to, and is not like, one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, which is the worship of idols, associating partners with Allah, and acting in disobedience to Allah. "And they followed their desires" in worshipping them, and they immersed themselves in kinds of misguidance without any doubt that would warrant suspicion, let alone a clear proof.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had explained the difference between the two groups in guidance and misguidance, He explained the difference in their destination and their end, so He said: ﴿The description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. The sentence is a new (resumptive) clause, to explain the excellences of the Garden and what is in it. The meaning of ﴿description (*mathal*)﴾ is its wondrous quality. It is the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: its supposed predicate is "what they hear." Sibawayh supposed it to be "what is recited to you is the description of the Garden." He said: *mathal* means description, and its meaning is "the description of the Garden." The clause ﴿therein are rivers of water unchanging﴾ etc. explains the *mathal*.

It was also said that *mathal* is superfluous. It was also said that ﴿the description of the Garden﴾ is the subject, and the predicate is "therein are rivers." It was also said that its predicate is ﴿like one who abides forever﴾.

*Al-asin* means "that which has changed." It is said: "the water became *asin* (آسِنَ) yā'sanu (يَأْسَنُ) *usūnan* (أُسُونًا)," when its smell has changed. Similar is *al-ājin* (الآجِنُ). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I shall leave the horn with its fingertips yellowed,*
*swaying on the spear like the swaying of brackish, changed water.*

The majority of readers recited *āsin* (آسِنٍ) with the long vowel (*madd*). Humayd and Ibn Kathir recited it with the short vowel (*qasr*); both are dialects, like *ḥādhir* and *ḥadhir*.

Al-Akhfash said: the long form is intended for the future, and the short form is intended for the present.

﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾: that is, it does not turn sour as the milk of this world does, because it did not come out from the udders of camels, sheep and cattle.

﴿And rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾: that is, delicious to them, pleasant to drink, which the drinkers do not find distasteful. It is said: *sharāb ladhdh* (شَرابٌ لَذٌّ) and *ladhīdh* (لَذِيذٌ), and *fīhi ladhdha* (فِيهِ لَذَّةٌ) with the same meaning. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers﴾ [al-Saffat: 46]. The majority recited *ladhdhatin* (لَذَّةٍ) with the genitive, as an adjective of *khamr*. It was also read with the accusative as a *masdar* or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). It was also read with the nominative as an adjective of *anhār*.

﴿And rivers of honey, purified﴾: that is, purified from what mixes with it of wax, debris, dregs and sediment. ﴿And for them therein is every kind of fruit﴾: that is, for the people of the Garden in the Garden, along with what has been mentioned of the drinks, is every kind of fruit; that is, every category of its categories. *Min* (مِن) is superfluous for emphasis. ﴿And forgiveness from their Lord﴾ for their sins. The indefiniteness of *maghfira* (مَغْفِرَةٌ) is for magnification: that is, for them is a great forgiveness, coming from their Lord.

﴿Like one who abides forever in the Fire﴾: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the supposed meaning is: "Is it then one who is in the bliss of the Garden in this description, abiding forever therein, like one who abides forever in the Fire?" Or it is the predicate of His saying "the description of the Garden," as preceded.

Al-Farra' preferred the first, saying: he intended "Is he who is in this bliss like one who abides forever in the Fire?"

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, "Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord, and is given these things, like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, and who abides forever in the Fire?" So His saying "like one" (كَمَن) is a substitution for His saying ﴿Is he for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾.

Ibn Kaysan said: the description of the Garden in which are fruits and rivers is not like the description of the Fire in which are boiling water and *zaqqum*; and the description of the people of the Garden in bliss is not like the description of the people of the Fire in painful torment.

His saying: ﴿and they are given boiling water to drink﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause (*silah*). He coordinated a verbal clause with a nominal clause, but he observed in the first the wording of *man* and in the second its meaning. *Hamim* is hot water of intense boiling. When they drink it, it cuts their intestines, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so that it cuts their bowels﴾, because of its extreme heat.

*Al-am'a'* is the plural of *ma'an* (مِعًى), and it is what is in the bellies of the intestines.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾: that is, among these disbelievers who enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, ﴿those who listen to you﴾, and they are the hypocrites. He made the pronoun singular in view of the wording of *man*, and plural in His saying ﴿until, when they go out from you﴾ in view of its meaning. The meaning is that the hypocrites used to attend the places of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) admonition and the occasions of his sermons, which he dictated to the Muslims, until, when they went out from him, ﴿they said to those who were given knowledge﴾. They were the scholars among the Companions. It was said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas; it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud; it was said: Abu al-Darda'. The first is preferred. That is, they asked the people of knowledge, and said to them: ﴿What did he say just now?﴾ That is, what did the Prophet say just now, in the manner of mockery. The meaning is: "We did not pay attention to his words." *Ānifan* (آنِفًا) is intended to mean "just now," the nearest of times. From it comes *amrun ānif* (أمْرٌ آنِفٌ), that is, a newly begun matter (مُسْتَأْنَفٌ) [p. 1375]; and *rawḍatun unuf* (رَوْضَةٌ أُنُفٌ), that is, a meadow no one has grazed. Its accusative is as an adverb of time: that is, a newly begun time; or it is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in *qāla* (قالَ).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *istannaftu al-shay'* (اسْتَأْنَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ), when you begin something. Its origin is taken from the nose (*anf*) of a thing, for what has preceded from it, borrowed from the organ. From it is the saying of the poet:

*And the secret of their neighbour is forbidden to them,*
*and their neighbour eats the nose of the dishes.*

The indication of His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to those mentioned of the hypocrites: ﴿those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾, so they do not believe, and their hearts do not turn toward any good; ﴿and they follow their desires﴾ in disbelief and obstinacy.

Then He mentioned the condition of their opposites, so He said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. That is, those who were guided to the path of good, so they believed in Allah and acted upon what He commanded them, He increased them in guidance by granting success. It was said: He increased them by the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: He increased them by the Qur'an.

Al-Farra' said: the turning away and mockery of the hypocrites increased them in guidance. It was said: the descent of the abrogating (*nāsikh*) [verse] increased them in guidance. In any case, the meaning is that He increased them in faith, knowledge and insight into the religion. ﴿And gave them their piety﴾: that is, He inspired them with it and helped them to it.

As for *taqwa* (piety), al-Rabi' said: it is fear (*khashya*). Al-Suddi said: it is the reward of the Hereafter. Muqatil said: it is the success to act in what He is pleased with. It was said: acting upon the abrogating [verse] and leaving the abrogated (*mansukh*) one. It was said: leaving the concessions (*rukhas*) and adhering to the firm obligations (*'azā'im*).

﴿Do they then await anything but the Hour﴾: that is, the Resurrection, ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾: that is, unexpectedly. In this there is a severe threat to the disbelievers. His saying ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾ is a substitution for "the Hour," a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*).

Abu Ja'far al-Rawwasi recited *in ta'tihim* (إنْ تَأْتِهِمْ) with the conditional *in* (إنْ). ﴿So its signs have already come﴾: that is, its indications and its marks. They had read in their books that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the last of the prophets, so his being sent is among its signs. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

*Al-ashrat* (الأشْراطُ) is the plural of *shart* (شَرْطٌ), with the *ra'* vowelled both with sukun and with fatha.

It was said: what is meant by "its signs" here is its causes, which are less than its greatest parts.

It was said: he intended by the signs of the Hour the splitting of the moon and the smoke; so said al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: the abundance of wealth and trade, false testimony, the severing of kinship ties, the scarcity of the noble and the abundance of the base. From it is the saying of Abu Zayd al-Aswad:

*If you have indeed resolved on severing between us,*
*then the signs of its beginning have already appeared.*

﴿Then how will there be for them, when their reminder comes to them?﴾ "Their reminder" (ذِكْراهم) is the subject, and its predicate is "then how will there be for them," that is: how will there be for them the remembrance when the Hour comes to them, as in His saying: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance be for him?﴾ [al-Fajr: 23]. And "when it comes to them" is a parenthetical clause between the subject and the predicate.

﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾: that is, if you know that the basis of good is monotheism and obedience, and the basis of evil is associating partners with Allah and acting in disobedience to Allah, then know that there is no god besides Him and no lord other than Him. The meaning is: "Remain firm upon that and persist in it," because he (ﷺ) had already known before this that there is no god but Allah. It was said: "what you know by inference, know it as certain knowledge." It was also said the meaning is: "Remember that there is no god but Allah," so he expressed remembrance by knowledge.

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾: that is, ask Allah forgiveness that any sin should occur from you, or ask Allah that He preserve you, or ask Him forgiveness for what may perhaps proceed from you of leaving the better course (*tark al-awla*).

It was said the address is to him, and the intended meaning is his community. This is rejected by His saying ﴿and for the believing men and believing women﴾, for its meaning is his asking forgiveness for the sins of his community by supplicating for them to be forgiven for what has passed of their sins.

﴿And Allah knows your movement﴾ in your deeds, ﴿and your resting place﴾ in the abode of the Hereafter. It was also said: your movement in your deeds by day, and your resting place in your night while you sleep.

It was said: your movement in the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers, and your resting place on the earth, that is, your dwelling in it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 29–31 (part 1 of 2):

The believers asked their Lord, mighty and majestic, to send down to His Messenger – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – a surah commanding them to fight the disbelievers, out of eagerness on their part for jihad (struggle in the way of Allah) and for attaining what Allah has prepared for the mujahidin (those who wage jihad) of abundant reward. Allah relates their statement, saying: ﴿And those who believe say, "Why has a surah not been sent down?"﴾, i.e., "Would that a surah had been sent down!" ﴿But when a decisive surah is sent down﴾, i.e., one not abrogated (naskh), ﴿and fighting is mentioned therein﴾, i.e., jihad is enjoined. Qatadah said: every surah in which jihad is mentioned is a decisive (muhkamah) surah, and it is the most severe of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (﴿But when a new surah is sent down﴾), i.e., newly revealed.

The majority read ﴿uni̇zilat﴾ (فَإذا أُنْزِلَتْ) and ﴿dhukira﴾ (وذُكِرَ) with both verbs in the passive voice.

Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn 'Umayr read ﴿nazalat﴾ (نَزَلَتْ), and ﴿dhakara﴾ (وذَكَرَ) with both verbs in the active voice, and the object ﴿al-qital﴾ (الْقِتالَ) in the accusative.

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, i.e., doubt, and they are the hypocrites, ﴿looking at you with the look of one fainting from death﴾, i.e., they look at you with the look of one whose gaze becomes fixed at the time of death, out of their cowardice regarding fighting and their inclination toward the disbelievers.

Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said: he means that they fix their eyes upon you and look at you intensely, as the one whose gaze is fixed at death does. ﴿So woe to them (awla lahum)﴾. Al-Jawhari said: the saying "awla laka" is a threat and a warning; so also said Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Qatadah.

Al-Asma'i said: the meaning of their saying "awla laka" in threat is: may what you dislike come upon you and draw near to you (waliyaka wa-qaraba-ka ma takrahu). He recited the verse of the poet:

"He pressed between two of them, and was near (awla) to exceeding three."

That is: he came close to exceeding three.

Tha'lab said: nothing better has been said about (awla) than what al-Asma'i said.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is said to one who intended anger and then let it go: awla laka, i.e., you came close to anger.

Al-Jurjani said: it is derived from "al-wayl" (woe), i.e., "woe to them," and so said al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf.

Qatadah also said: it is as if he said, "Punishment is nearer (awla) to them."

His saying ﴿Obedience and fair speech﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, i.e., their affair is obedience, or obedience and fair speech are better for you.

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the estimated meaning is: "And obedience and fair speech are better and more fitting for you than other than them."

It was said that ﴿ta'ah﴾ (طاعَةٌ) is the predicate of ﴿awla﴾, it was said that ﴿ta'ah﴾ is an attribute of ﴿surah﴾, and it was said that ﴿lahum﴾ is a fronted predicate and ﴿ta'ah﴾ a delayed subject; the first is preferable.

﴿So when the matter is resolved (ʿazama al-amr)﴾: ʿazama al-amr means the matter became serious, i.e., fighting became serious, and became obligatory and was enjoined. He attributed the resolve (al-ʿazm) to the matter, while it belongs to its people, as a metaphor (majaz). The response of "idha" (when) is said to be ﴿then if they had been truthful with Allah﴾, and it was said to be omitted, its estimate being "they disliked it."

The exegetes said its meaning is: when the matter became serious and the obligation of fighting was binding, they opposed and held back. ﴿Then if they had been truthful with Allah﴾ in displaying faith and obedience, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ than disobedience and opposition.

﴿So would you, if you turned away, perhaps cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ This is an address to those in whose hearts is a disease, by way of iltifat (shift of address), for greater rebuke and reproach.

Al-Kalbi said: i.e., would you, if you took charge of the affairs of the community, perhaps cause corruption in the land through injustice? Ka'b said: ﴿cause corruption in the land﴾, i.e., by killing one another. Qatadah said: if you turn away from obedience to the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, you will cause corruption in the land by shedding blood and severing your ties of kinship. Ibn Juraij said: if you turn away from obedience. It was said: you turn away from fighting and separate from its rulings.

The majority read ﴿tawallaytum﴾ (تَوَلَّيْتُمْ) in the active voice. Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with a ḍammah on the tā' and wāw and a kasrah on the lām, in the passive voice, and Ibn Abi Ishaq, Warsh, from Ya'qub, also read it thus. Its meaning: would you, if rulers who are oppressors were put in charge over you, perhaps rebel against them in strife, fight them, and sever your ties of kinship through transgression, injustice and killing.

The majority read ﴿wa-tuqatti'u﴾ (وتُقَطِّعُوا) with the doubled (intensive) form for multiplicity, while Abu 'Amr in one narration from him, Sallam, ʿIsa and Ya'qub read it with the single form from qata' (cutting). It is said: ʿasaytu an af'ala kadha (عَسَيْتُ أنْ أفْعَلَ كَذا), and ʿasaytu with fatḥah and kasrah are two dialects, as mentioned by al-Jawhari and others. The predicate of ﴿ʿasaytum﴾ is ﴿an tufsidu﴾, and the conditional clause between them is a parenthetical insertion.

The reference of ﴿ulaʾika﴾ (أُولَئِكَ) is to those addressed in what preceded, and it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿Those whom Allah has cursed﴾, i.e., He removed them far from His mercy and expelled them from it, ﴿and has made them deaf﴾ to hearing the truth, ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ from seeing what they would use as evidence for the Oneness (tawhid), the resurrection, and the truth of all that the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – called them to.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ is for denunciation (inkar). The meaning: do they not understand it, so that they would know, by what it contains of restraining admonitions, manifest proofs and decisive demonstrations, which suffice anyone who has understanding and intellect, and which restrain him from disbelief in Allah, associating partners with Him, and acting upon His disobediences? ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ (am here is the disjunctive am), i.e., rather, are there locks upon their hearts, so that they do not understand and do not reason?

Muqatil said: he means the sealing (tab') upon the hearts. "Locks" is a metaphor for the closing of the heart against knowledge of the truth. The idafah (construct) of "locks" to "hearts" serves to draw attention to the fact that what is meant is what for the hearts is like locks for doors. The meaning of the verse is that faith does not enter their hearts, and disbelief and polytheism do not leave them, because Allah, glorified is He, has sealed them; and what is meant by these hearts is the hearts of these addressees.

The majority read ﴿aqfaluha﴾ (أقْفالُها) in the plural, and it was read ﴿iqfaluha﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun like iqbal.

﴿Indeed, those who reverted on their heels (irtaddu ʿala adbarihim)﴾, i.e., returned to disbelief as they were before. Qatadah said: they are the disbelievers of the People of the Book, who disbelieved in the Prophet – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – after they had recognized his description among them; and Ibn Jarir said likewise. al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: they are the hypocrites who sat out from fighting. This is more preferable, because the context concerns the hypocrites. ﴿After guidance had become clear to them﴾ through what the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – brought them of manifest miracles and clear proofs. ﴿Satan has enticed them﴾, i.e., he adorned their sins for them and made it easy for them to fall into them. This clause is the predicate of "inna." The meaning of ﴿and prolonged their hopes (wa-amla lahum)﴾ is that Satan extended for them in hope and promised them long life. It was said: the one who prolonged for them is Allah, mighty and majestic, in the sense that He did not hasten the punishment upon them.

The majority read ﴿amla﴾ in the active voice, while Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read it in the passive voice. It was said: according to this reading the agent is Allah or Satan, as in the first reading; al-Farra', al-Mufaddal chose that the agent is Allah, but the better choice is that it is Satan, due to the nearness of his mention.

The reference of ﴿that﴾ (ذَلِكَ) is to the apostasy mentioned earlier; it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿because they said to those who hated what Allah had sent down﴾, and they are the polytheists, ﴿"We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾, and this part is enmity toward the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – and opposition to what he brought.

It was said: the meaning is that the hypocrites said to the Jews, "We will obey you in part of the matter." It was said that the ones speaking are the Jews, and "those who hated what Allah sent down" are the hypocrites. It was said that the reference of "that" is to the respite (imla'), and it was said to the enticement (taswil). The first is preferable.

What supports that the speakers are the hypocrites and the haters are the Jews is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who are hypocritical, who say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieve, "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you"﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. And since their saying mentioned here, to those who hated what Allah sent down, was in secret among themselves, Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And Allah knows their secrets (israrahum)﴾. The majority read the hamzah with a fatḥah, as the plural of sirr (secret), and this reading was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

The Kufans, Hamzah, al-Nasa'i, Hafs from ʿAsim, Ibn Wththab and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the hamzah as a verbal noun, i.e., their concealment (ikhfa'ahum).

﴿Then how will it be when the angels take them in death (tawaffathum al-malaikah)?﴾ The fa' indicates that what follows results from what precedes, and "kayfa" is in the nominative position as a fronted predicate; the estimate being: "then how is His knowledge of their secrets when the angels take them in death?" Or it is in the accusative position by an omitted verb, i.e., "then how will they act?" Or it is the predicate of an estimated "kana" (was/will be): i.e., "then how will they be?" and the temporal clause is connected to the estimated element. The majority read ﴿tawaffathum﴾, while al-A'mash read ﴿tawaffahum﴾. The clause ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿tawaffathum﴾ or from its object: i.e., striking their faces and striking their backs. In the statement there is intimidation and severity; the meaning is that if the punishment is delayed from them, their condition will be this, and it is a depiction of their death in the worst and most hideous state.

It was said: this occurs at the time of fighting, as support from the angels for the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – and it was said: this occurs on the Day of Resurrection; the first is preferable.

The reference of ﴿that﴾ is to the aforementioned taking in death in the described manner; it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿because they followed what angered Allah﴾, i.e., because of their following what provokes Allah's anger of disbelief and sins. It was said: their concealment of what is in the Torah concerning the description of our Prophet – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. The first is preferable because of the generality of the wording. ﴿And they disliked His pleasure﴾, i.e., they disliked what Allah is pleased with of faith, monotheism and obedience, so Allah nullified their deeds for this reason. By "their deeds" is meant the deeds whose form is the form of obedience; otherwise there is no deed for a disbeliever, or it refers to the good they had done before the apostasy.

﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their rancor?﴾ This refers to the hypocrites mentioned earlier, and "am" is the disjunctive am, i.e., rather, do the hypocrites think ﴿that Allah will not bring forth their spite (adghanahum)﴾? Ikhraj (bringing forth) means manifestation, and adghan is the plural of dighn, which is what is concealed of hatred.

It has been disputed concerning its meaning: it was said it is deceit, it was said envy, it was said malice. Al-Jawhari said: al-dighn and al-daghina are malice. Qutrub said: in the verse it is enmity. And "an" is the lightened form of the heavy one, whose noun is an estimated pronoun of the matter.

﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you (la-arayнakahum)﴾, i.e., We would have made you know them and identified them to you by their very persons, with a knowledge that stands in place of seeing. The Arabs say: "I will show you what I will do," i.e., I will inform you. ﴿Then you would have recognized them by their marks (bi-simahum)﴾, i.e., by their particular sign by which they are distinguished.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that if We willed, We would have placed upon the hypocrites a sign, which is the mark (sima), and you would have recognized them by that sign. The fa' indicates the recognition following upon the will, and what comes after it is conjoined to the response of "law." The repetition in the conjoined element is for emphasis. As for the lam in ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of speech (lahn al-qawl)﴾, it is the response to an omitted oath.

The exegetes said: lahn al-qawl is its implication, its intent, its import, and what they allude to of disparaging your affair and the affair of the Muslims. After this, no hypocrite spoke in his presence without his understanding it.

Abu Zayd said: "lahanta lahu al-lahn" means when you say to him a saying which he understands from you while it remains hidden from others. From it is the poet's saying:

"A speech that is correct, and at times you allude (talḥanu)."
"And the best speech is that which is allusive (laḥnan)," i.e., its best is that which is an allusion that the addressee understands and others do not, owing to his acuteness and intelligence. The root of lahn is the inclining of speech toward one of the ways for some purpose.

﴿And Allah knows your deeds﴾, none of them is hidden from Him, so He will requite you for them, and in this is severe warning.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 47, verses 29–31 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and those who are patient.﴾ That is, He will deal with you as one who tests, by commanding you to fight, until He knows who obeys the command to fight and endures patiently in his religion and in the hardships of what he has been charged with.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the three verbs with the nun (nun of the first person plural). Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read them all with the ya' (third person). The meaning of ﴿and We will test your affairs (akhbar)﴾ is that We will make them manifest and expose them, as a trial for you, so that it becomes clear to the people who obeys what Allah has commanded him, who disobeys, and who does not comply.

The majority read ﴿wa-nabluwa﴾ with a fatha on the waw, as a conjunction (‘atf) upon His words ﴿until We know﴾. Warsh, on the authority of Ya'qub, related it with a sukun on the waw, as a new sentence (qat') cut off from what precedes it.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the creation, and finished with them, the kinship (al-rahim) stood up and clung to the loins (hiqw) of the Most Merciful. He said: 'Enough.' It said: 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.' He said: 'Yes. Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever from whoever severs from you?' It said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is for you.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, perhaps cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ up to His words ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾" The narrations concerning the maintenance of kinship are very numerous.

Ibn Jarir related, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾, that he said: "They are the people of hypocrisy (nifaq)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His words ﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their malice?﴾, that he said: "Their deeds, their corruption, and the envy that is in their hearts. Then Allah, the Exalted, afterwards pointed out the hypocrites to the Prophet (ﷺ), so he would call them by the names of men from among the people of hypocrisy."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, regarding His words ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech (lahn al-qawl)﴾, that he said: "By their hatred of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib."

Allah relates their statement, saying: ﴿And those who believe say, "Why has a surah not been sent down?"﴾, i.e., "Would that a surah had been sent down!" ﴿But when a decisive surah is sent down﴾, i.e., one not abrogated (naskh), ﴿and fighting is mentioned therein﴾, i.e., jihad is enjoined. Qatadah said: every surah in which jihad is mentioned is a decisive (muhkamah) surah, and it is the most severe of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. The Kufans, Hamzah, al-Nasa'i, Hafs from ʿAsim, Ibn Wththab and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the hamzah as a verbal noun, i.e., their concealment (ikhfa'ahum).

﴿Then how will it be when the angels take them in death (tawaffathum al-malaikah)?﴾ The fa' indicates that what follows results from what precedes, and "kayfa" is in the nominative position as a fronted predicate; the estimate being: "then how is His knowledge of their secrets when the angels take them in death?" Or it is in the accusative position by an omitted verb, i.e., "then how will they act?" Or it is the predicate of an estimated "kana" (was/will be): i.e., "then how will they be?" and the temporal clause is connected to the estimated element. The majority read ﴿tawaffathum﴾, while al-A'mash read ﴿tawaffahum﴾. The clause ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿tawaffathum﴾ or from its object: i.e., striking their faces and striking their backs. In the statement there is intimidation and severity; the meaning is that if the punishment is delayed from them, their condition will be this, and it is a depiction of their death in the worst and most hideous state.

It was said: this occurs at the time of fighting, as support from the angels for the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – and it was said: this occurs on the Day of Resurrection; the first is preferable.

The reference of ﴿that﴾ is to the aforementioned taking in death in the described manner; it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿because they followed what angered Allah﴾, i.e., because of their following what provokes Allah's anger of disbelief and sins. It was said: their concealment of what is in the Torah concerning the description of our Prophet – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. The first is preferable because of the generality of the wording. ﴿And they disliked His pleasure﴾, i.e., they disliked what Allah is pleased with of faith, monotheism and obedience, so Allah nullified their deeds for this reason. By "their deeds" is meant the deeds whose form is the form of obedience; otherwise there is no deed for a disbeliever, or it refers to the good they had done before the apostasy.

﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their rancor?﴾ This refers to the hypocrites mentioned earlier, and "am" is the disjunctive am, i.e., rather, do the hypocrites think ﴿that Allah will not bring forth their spite (adghanahum)﴾? Ikhraj (bringing forth) means manifestation, and adghan is the plural of dighn, which is what is concealed of hatred.

It has been disputed concerning its meaning: it was said it is deceit, it was said envy, it was said malice. Al-Jawhari said: al-dighn and al-daghina are malice. Qutrub said: in the verse it is enmity. And "an" is the lightened form of the heavy one, whose noun is an estimated pronoun of the matter.

﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you (la-arayнakahum)﴾, i.e., We would have made you know them and identified them to you by their very persons, with a knowledge that stands in place of seeing. The Arabs say: "I will show you what I will do," i.e., I will inform you. ﴿Then you would have recognized them by their marks (bi-simahum)﴾, i.e., by their particular sign by which they are distinguished.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that if We willed, We would have placed upon the hypocrites a sign, which is the mark (sima), and you would have recognized them by that sign. The fa' indicates the recognition following upon the will, and what comes after it is conjoined to the response of "law." The repetition in the conjoined element is for emphasis. As for the lam in ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of speech (lahn al-qawl)﴾, it is the response to an omitted oath.

The exegetes said: lahn al-qawl is its implication, its intent, its import, and what they allude to of disparaging your affair and the affair of the Muslims. After this, no hypocrite spoke in his presence without his understanding it.

Abu Zayd said: "lahanta lahu al-lahn" means when you say to him a saying which he understands from you while it remains hidden from others. From it is the poet's saying:

"A speech that is correct, and at times you allude (talḥanu)."
"And the best speech is that which is allusive (laḥnan)," i.e., its best is that which is an allusion that the addressee understands and others do not, owing to his acuteness and intelligence. The root of lahn is the inclining of speech toward one of the ways for some purpose.

﴿And Allah knows your deeds﴾, none of them is hidden from Him, so He will requite you for them, and in this is severe warning.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 47, verses 29–31 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and those who are patient.﴾ That is, He will deal with you as one who tests, by commanding you to fight, until He knows who obeys the command to fight and endures patiently in his religion and in the hardships of what he has been charged with.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the three verbs with the nun (nun of the first person plural). Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read them all with the ya' (third person). The meaning of ﴿and We will test your affairs (akhbar)﴾ is that We will make them manifest and expose them, as a trial for you, so that it becomes clear to the people who obeys what Allah has commanded him, who disobeys, and who does not comply.

The majority read ﴿wa-nabluwa﴾ with a fatha on the waw, as a conjunction (‘atf) upon His words ﴿until We know﴾. Warsh, on the authority of Ya'qub, related it with a sukun on the waw, as a new sentence (qat') cut off from what precedes it.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the creation, and finished with them, the kinship (al-rahim) stood up and clung to the loins (hiqw) of the Most Merciful. He said: 'Enough.' It said: 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.' He said: 'Yes. Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever from whoever severs from you?' It said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is for you.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, perhaps cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ up to His words ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾" The narrations concerning the maintenance of kinship are very numerous.

Ibn Jarir related, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾, that he said: "They are the people of hypocrisy (nifaq)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His words ﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their malice?﴾, that he said: "Their deeds, their corruption, and the envy that is in their hearts. Then Allah, the Exalted, afterwards pointed out the hypocrites to the Prophet (ﷺ), so he would call them by the names of men from among the people of hypocrisy."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, regarding His words ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech (lahn al-qawl)﴾, that he said: "By their hatred of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 47, verses 29–31 (part 1 of 2):

The believers asked their Lord, mighty and majestic, to send down to His Messenger – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – a surah commanding them to fight the disbelievers, out of eagerness on their part for jihad (struggle in the way of Allah) and for attaining what Allah has prepared for the mujahidin (those who wage jihad) of abundant reward. Allah relates their statement, saying: ﴿And those who believe say, "Why has a surah not been sent down?"﴾, i.e., "Would that a surah had been sent down!" ﴿But when a decisive surah is sent down﴾, i.e., one not abrogated (naskh), ﴿and fighting is mentioned therein﴾, i.e., jihad is enjoined. Qatadah said: every surah in which jihad is mentioned is a decisive (muhkamah) surah, and it is the most severe of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (﴿But when a new surah is sent down﴾), i.e., newly revealed.

The majority read ﴿uni̇zilat﴾ (فَإذا أُنْزِلَتْ) and ﴿dhukira﴾ (وذُكِرَ) with both verbs in the passive voice.

Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn 'Umayr read ﴿nazalat﴾ (نَزَلَتْ), and ﴿dhakara﴾ (وذَكَرَ) with both verbs in the active voice, and the object ﴿al-qital﴾ (الْقِتالَ) in the accusative.

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, i.e., doubt, and they are the hypocrites, ﴿looking at you with the look of one fainting from death﴾, i.e., they look at you with the look of one whose gaze becomes fixed at the time of death, out of their cowardice regarding fighting and their inclination toward the disbelievers.

Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said: he means that they fix their eyes upon you and look at you intensely, as the one whose gaze is fixed at death does. ﴿So woe to them (awla lahum)﴾. Al-Jawhari said: the saying "awla laka" is a threat and a warning; so also said Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Qatadah.

Al-Asma'i said: the meaning of their saying "awla laka" in threat is: may what you dislike come upon you and draw near to you (waliyaka wa-qaraba-ka ma takrahu). He recited the verse of the poet:

"He pressed between two of them, and was near (awla) to exceeding three."

That is: he came close to exceeding three.

Tha'lab said: nothing better has been said about (awla) than what al-Asma'i said.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is said to one who intended anger and then let it go: awla laka, i.e., you came close to anger.

Al-Jurjani said: it is derived from "al-wayl" (woe), i.e., "woe to them," and so said al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf.

Qatadah also said: it is as if he said, "Punishment is nearer (awla) to them."

His saying ﴿Obedience and fair speech﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, i.e., their affair is obedience, or obedience and fair speech are better for you.

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the estimated meaning is: "And obedience and fair speech are better and more fitting for you than other than them."

It was said that ﴿ta'ah﴾ (طاعَةٌ) is the predicate of ﴿awla﴾, it was said that ﴿ta'ah﴾ is an attribute of ﴿surah﴾, and it was said that ﴿lahum﴾ is a fronted predicate and ﴿ta'ah﴾ a delayed subject; the first is preferable.

﴿So when the matter is resolved (ʿazama al-amr)﴾: ʿazama al-amr means the matter became serious, i.e., fighting became serious, and became obligatory and was enjoined. He attributed the resolve (al-ʿazm) to the matter, while it belongs to its people, as a metaphor (majaz). The response of "idha" (when) is said to be ﴿then if they had been truthful with Allah﴾, and it was said to be omitted, its estimate being "they disliked it."

The exegetes said its meaning is: when the matter became serious and the obligation of fighting was binding, they opposed and held back. ﴿Then if they had been truthful with Allah﴾ in displaying faith and obedience, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ than disobedience and opposition.

﴿So would you, if you turned away, perhaps cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ This is an address to those in whose hearts is a disease, by way of iltifat (shift of address), for greater rebuke and reproach.

Al-Kalbi said: i.e., would you, if you took charge of the affairs of the community, perhaps cause corruption in the land through injustice? Ka'b said: ﴿cause corruption in the land﴾, i.e., by killing one another. Qatadah said: if you turn away from obedience to the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, you will cause corruption in the land by shedding blood and severing your ties of kinship. Ibn Juraij said: if you turn away from obedience. It was said: you turn away from fighting and separate from its rulings.

The majority read ﴿tawallaytum﴾ (تَوَلَّيْتُمْ) in the active voice. Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with a ḍammah on the tā' and wāw and a kasrah on the lām, in the passive voice, and Ibn Abi Ishaq, Warsh, from Ya'qub, also read it thus. Its meaning: would you, if rulers who are oppressors were put in charge over you, perhaps rebel against them in strife, fight them, and sever your ties of kinship through transgression, injustice and killing.

The majority read ﴿wa-tuqatti'u﴾ (وتُقَطِّعُوا) with the doubled (intensive) form for multiplicity, while Abu 'Amr in one narration from him, Sallam, ʿIsa and Ya'qub read it with the single form from qata' (cutting). It is said: ʿasaytu an af'ala kadha (عَسَيْتُ أنْ أفْعَلَ كَذا), and ʿasaytu with fatḥah and kasrah are two dialects, as mentioned by al-Jawhari and others. The predicate of ﴿ʿasaytum﴾ is ﴿an tufsidu﴾, and the conditional clause between them is a parenthetical insertion.

The reference of ﴿ulaʾika﴾ (أُولَئِكَ) is to those addressed in what preceded, and it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿Those whom Allah has cursed﴾, i.e., He removed them far from His mercy and expelled them from it, ﴿and has made them deaf﴾ to hearing the truth, ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ from seeing what they would use as evidence for the Oneness (tawhid), the resurrection, and the truth of all that the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – called them to.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ is for denunciation (inkar). The meaning: do they not understand it, so that they would know, by what it contains of restraining admonitions, manifest proofs and decisive demonstrations, which suffice anyone who has understanding and intellect, and which restrain him from disbelief in Allah, associating partners with Him, and acting upon His disobediences? ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ (am here is the disjunctive am), i.e., rather, are there locks upon their hearts, so that they do not understand and do not reason?

Muqatil said: he means the sealing (tab') upon the hearts. "Locks" is a metaphor for the closing of the heart against knowledge of the truth. The idafah (construct) of "locks" to "hearts" serves to draw attention to the fact that what is meant is what for the hearts is like locks for doors. The meaning of the verse is that faith does not enter their hearts, and disbelief and polytheism do not leave them, because Allah, glorified is He, has sealed them; and what is meant by these hearts is the hearts of these addressees.

The majority read ﴿aqfaluha﴾ (أقْفالُها) in the plural, and it was read ﴿iqfaluha﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun like iqbal.

﴿Indeed, those who reverted on their heels (irtaddu ʿala adbarihim)﴾, i.e., returned to disbelief as they were before. Qatadah said: they are the disbelievers of the People of the Book, who disbelieved in the Prophet – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – after they had recognized his description among them; and Ibn Jarir said likewise. al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: they are the hypocrites who sat out from fighting. This is more preferable, because the context concerns the hypocrites. ﴿After guidance had become clear to them﴾ through what the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – brought them of manifest miracles and clear proofs. ﴿Satan has enticed them﴾, i.e., he adorned their sins for them and made it easy for them to fall into them. This clause is the predicate of "inna." The meaning of ﴿and prolonged their hopes (wa-amla lahum)﴾ is that Satan extended for them in hope and promised them long life. It was said: the one who prolonged for them is Allah, mighty and majestic, in the sense that He did not hasten the punishment upon them.

The majority read ﴿amla﴾ in the active voice, while Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read it in the passive voice. It was said: according to this reading the agent is Allah or Satan, as in the first reading; al-Farra', al-Mufaddal chose that the agent is Allah, but the better choice is that it is Satan, due to the nearness of his mention.

The reference of ﴿that﴾ (ذَلِكَ) is to the apostasy mentioned earlier; it is the subject, whose predicate is: ﴿because they said to those who hated what Allah had sent down﴾, and they are the polytheists, ﴿"We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾, and this part is enmity toward the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – and opposition to what he brought.

It was said: the meaning is that the hypocrites said to the Jews, "We will obey you in part of the matter." It was said that the ones speaking are the Jews, and "those who hated what Allah sent down" are the hypocrites. It was said that the reference of "that" is to the respite (imla'), and it was said to the enticement (taswil). The first is preferable.

What supports that the speakers are the hypocrites and the haters are the Jews is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who are hypocritical, who say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieve, "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you"﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 47, verses 32–38**

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾. By "these" is meant the hypocrites. It was also said: the People of the Book. And it was said: they are the disbelievers among the Quraysh who fed [the troops] on the day of Badr.

The meaning of "barring them from the way of Allah" is their preventing people from Islam and from following the Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning of ﴿and opposed the Messenger﴾ is that they showed enmity towards him and contradicted him, ﴿after guidance had become clear to them﴾, meaning they knew that he (ﷺ) was a prophet from Allah, through the clear miracles they witnessed and the decisive proofs. ﴿They will not harm Allah at all﴾ by their refusal to believe and their persistence in disbelief; they harm only themselves. ﴿And He will render their deeds void﴾, meaning He will nullify them. By "these deeds" is meant what has the outward form of good deeds, such as feeding people, maintaining ties of kinship, and all the other good they used to do, even though these are void from the outset because disbelief is an impediment. It was also said: by "deeds" is meant the schemes they set up to nullify the religion of Allah and the plots they sought to carry out against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His believing servants to obey Him and to obey His Messenger, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ in what you have been commanded of the laws mentioned in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Then He forbade them from nullifying their deeds, as the disbelievers nullified theirs by persisting in disbelief, saying: ﴿And do not nullify your deeds.﴾ Al-Hasan said: meaning, do not nullify your good deeds by acts of disobedience.

Al-Zuhri said: by major sins.

Al-Kalbi and Ibn Jurayj said: by showing off and seeking reputation.

Muqatil said: by reminding [others of one's favours] (al-mann).

The apparent meaning is a prohibition against every cause among the causes that lead to the nullification of deeds, whatever it may be, without restricting it to a specific type.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that He does not forgive those who persist in disbelief and in barring [others] from the way of Allah, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah, then die while they are disbelievers — never will Allah forgive them.﴾ He restricted the non-forgiveness to dying in disbelief, because the door of repentance and the path of forgiveness are not closed to one who is still alive. It was also said: by "deeds" is meant the schemes they set up to nullify the religion of Allah and the plots they sought to carry out against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-Kalbi and Ibn Jurayj said: by showing off and seeking reputation.

Muqatil said: by reminding [others of one's favours] (al-mann).

The apparent meaning is a prohibition against every cause among the causes that lead to the nullification of deeds, whatever it may be, without restricting it to a specific type.

﴿And Allah is the Rich﴾, the absolute one who is exempt from any need for your wealth, ﴿while you are the poor in need of Allah﴾ and of what He has of good and mercy. The clause ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾ is coordinated with the preceding conditional, which is ﴿And if you believe﴾. The meaning is: if you turn away from faith and piety, He will replace you with other people who will take your place and who are more obedient to Allah than you. ﴿Then they will not be like you﴾ in turning away from faith and piety.

'Ikrimah said: they are Persia and the Romans.

Al-Hasan said: they are the non-Arabs ('ajam).

Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd said: they are the people of Yemen. It was also said: the Ansar; and it was said: the angels; and it was said: the Successors (tabi'un).

Mujahid said: they are whomever Allah wills from among the rest of mankind.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of ﴿then they will not be like you﴾ is in stinginess with spending in the way of Allah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Muhammad ibn Nasr in the Book of Prayer, and Ibn Abi Hatim, reported from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to think that no sin would harm one who says "There is no god but Allah," just as no deed benefits one who associates partners with Allah, until this was revealed: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and do not nullify your deeds.﴾ So they feared that sin would nullify the deed. The wording of 'Abd ibn Humayd is: they feared that the major sins would nullify their deeds.

Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: We, the company of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), used to think that none of the good deeds is unaccepted, until this was revealed: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and do not nullify your deeds.﴾ When this verse was revealed, we said: what is this that nullifies our deeds? We said: the major sins that bring their own penalties, and the grave sins. So whenever we saw someone who had committed any of them, we said: he has been ruined. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whomever He wills﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:48). When it was revealed, we restrained ourselves from speaking about that, and whenever we saw someone who had committed any of them, we feared for him, and if he had not committed any of them, we hoped for him.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning his saying ("yatirakum," يَتِرَكُمْ), that he said: "When ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾ was revealed, they said: who are these? Salman was beside the Prophet (ﷺ), so he said: They are the Persians — this one and his people."

In its chain is Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji, who was alone in narrating it, and concerning him there is a well-known criticism.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported it from him, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾. They said: O Messenger of Allah, who are these people who, if we turn away, will be substituted for us and then will not be like us? So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Salman on the shoulder and said: This one and his people. By Him in whose hand my soul is, if faith were suspended from the Pleiades, men from Persia would reach it."

In its chain also is Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji.

Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar narration from the hadith of Jabir.
